excerpts:

Alaska reports 4 new mpox cases in Anchorage

Robert Herriman
Nov 09, 2026
Share
Alaska public health officials report three confirmed cases of mpox (monkeypox) in Anchorage in October 2026. All three patients are male, and an epidemiologic link has been identified only between the first two cases. None of the patients reported out-of-state travel.
The first two cases were caused by clade Ib mpox, marking the first reported cases of clade I mpox in Alaska; clade determination for the third case is pending. One patient was hospitalized briefly. All three patients are currently isolating and recovering. The investigation is ongoing.
Emerging Infectious Diseases and Global Health Security
A fourth case was reported to state officials on Thursday - there are now four mpox cases in Anchorage.
The global mpox outbreak that began in 2022 was caused by clade IIb. Since March 2026, imported cases of clade I mpox have increased, and presumed local transmission has been reported in 15 U.S. jurisdictions since August 2026. Historically, clade I has been associated with greater disease severity and higher casefatality ratios than clade II. However, recent clade I outbreaks have demonstrated substantially lower mortality, particularly when appropriate medical care is available.
Alaska health officials are encouraging anyone considered to be at risk of infection to get vaccinated.
The JYNNEOS vaccine, approved by the Food and Drug Administration in 2019, guards against both clades of mpox.

Experts told us the cases collectively show federal agents running roughshod over the constitutional rights of citizens. We found more than 100 Americans who were questioned about their citizenship, 63 Americans detained while recording, 36 Americans held for at least a day without being able to contact a lawyer or

process, equal protection, and freedom from unreasonable search and seizure, and request transparency regarding the Department’s actions,” the representatives wrote in their letter to DHS.
DHS has long insisted it is not arresting U.S. citizens, and it defended its immigration operations as “highly targeted.”

Last year, congressional Democrats announced a wide-ranging investigation into immigration agents’ detention of U.S. citizens in response to our earlier reporting that found that more than 170 citizens were detained by immigration agents .
Last month, Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, a New Mexico Democrat, introduced a bill, Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act, that would make it easier for citizens to sue immigration agents for wrongful arrests.
